messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 36-year-old retail manager, came to therapy at his wife’s insistence. He described a constant, humming anxiety that had become the backdrop to his life since the music festival eight months ago. The event itself he rarely spoke of, but it lived inside him not as a story, but as a series of stark, silent photographs. One was of a terrified woman’s face, mouth open in a scream he couldn’t hear over the roar of the crowd. Another was the rough, synthetic weave of a cheap blue windbreaker pressed so hard against his cheek he could feel the fabric’s grid pattern on his skin. These images felt more real to him than his memory of breakfast that morning; they were high-definition intrusions into the blur of his daily life.

The festival tragedy occurred when a panicked surge of people, reacting to a mistaken report of danger, created a deadly crowd crush near a narrow exit tunnel. David was pinned for what felt like an eternity, unable to move, the weight of bodies pressing in from all sides. He remembers the collective loss of control, the way people climbing over others became a form of misbehavior born of pure survival instinct. He had survived, but the memory of his own helplessness, of being unable to aid the man crushed beside him, had planted a seed of profound shame that grew with every recall of the event. When these snapshot memories surfaced, the shame was so acute it felt like a physical sickness, a hot flush spreading from his chest outwards.

His job at a large electronics store, once a source of pride, had become a minefield. The physical proximity of shoppers on a busy Saturday was enough to make his heart pound. A customer pushing impatiently through an aisle would trigger a cascade. The sight of this minor transgression, this everyday selfishness, would instantly flash one of the frozen images into his mind: the blue windbreaker, the screaming woman. The memory would arrive unbidden, sharp and visceral. To manage the sudden terror, David developed a set of desperate rituals. He would try to force the thought out, mentally shouting over it with inventory numbers or sales targets. He would tell himself it wasn't that bad, that it didn't really happen that way, a flimsy shield of magical thinking against an overwhelming reality.

This constant battle to suppress the memories only seemed to make them stronger and more frequent. The effort of pushing them down made him hyper-aware of his surroundings, constantly scanning for the triggers he knew would bring them on. When a memory did break through, he would retreat to the stockroom and dig the nails of his right hand deep into the palm of his left, the sharp, grounding pain a welcome distraction from the shame and fear. The brief relief it provided was his only reliable escape, but it left crescent-shaped marks his wife eventually noticed.

The cycle was relentless and self-perpetuating. A trigger, like feeling the rough texture of a customer’s jacket as they brushed past, would immediately bring forth a memory fragment. The shame-filled memory would, in turn, compel him to use his coping strategies, like suppressing the thought or finding a moment alone to hurt himself. These very strategies, however, sensitized him further. The more he tried not to think about it, the more he found himself scanning crowds, watching for any sign of people misbehaving, making the world outside his home feel increasingly dangerous and his own mind an unreliable narrator. The memories themselves fed his vigilance; after a particularly vivid flashback, he would be on high alert for hours, interpreting every close interaction as a potential threat. He started avoiding the sales floor during peak hours, a move that was beginning to affect his performance and draw questions from his regional manager. He came to therapy because he could no longer keep the two worlds separate; the silent, flashing images from the past were starting to cost him his present.
